In any case, as Hegel and Marx say, human beings, insofar as they are human, are always dialectical.
So if we want to understand what dialectic is and what its three fundamental categories are, we must look at how they appear in human beings.

Before doing that, however, we should remain a little longer with the purely formal side of dialectic and see what thesis, antithesis, and synthesis are independently of what they actually realize in human beings, in humanity, and in history.
As we already know, every dialectic rests on negativity.
And from a formal point of view, negativity is nothing other than negation.
If we use the letter A for the thesis, in which identity predominates, then we should use non-A for the antithesis, in which negativity predominates.
We can then say that every dialectic rests, formally, on the principle “discovered” by Hegel that:

In other words, the antithesis, although it appears as the negation of the thesis, is not nothing. It is something—something fully determinate, with a content just as clearly defined and positive as the content of the thesis.
So-called formal logic always has an ontological significance. It always rests on a particular conception of being.
Classical or pre-Hegelian formal logic was based exclusively—usually without being aware of it—on non-dialectical being.
Its first fundamental law was therefore the so-called law of identity:
According to this law, every concept, and every being or existence expressed by that concept, is always equal to itself.
This law is accompanied by a second, the law of non-contradiction, according to which one and the same concept—or being—cannot simultaneously be both A and non-A.
To these two laws, which fundamentally say the same thing, formal logic adds a third and final fundamental law: the law of excluded middle.
Every concept—or being—is always either A or non-A, and can never be anything else.

Formal, non-dialectical logic applies all three of these laws to one and the same concept or being—in fact, to any concept or being whatsoever. Dialectical logic works differently. It keeps the “law of identity” (A = A), but applies it only to the thesis. The purely negative law traditionally called the “law of non-contradiction” (A = non-non-A) becomes positive in dialectical logic and is applied to the antithesis.

In other words, dialectical logic assumes that a concept or being can be both A and non-A at once—though obviously not in exactly the same respect. Insofar as “identity” predominates, that is, insofar as it is a thesis, the concept or being is indeed equal to A. But as an antithesis, insofar as “negativity” predominates, it is also equal to non-A.

As non-A, it is of course no longer A but something else: B. Yet insofar as it is still the same being, it cannot be merely this completely different B. It must also be something other than B, something that remains connected in some way with A. It is therefore a third thing, C.

This is why dialectical logic replaces the law of the “excluded third” with a law of the “included third,” applying it to synthesis. In the end, the concept is neither simply A, the thesis, nor simply non-A, the antithesis or B. It is C, a third term: the synthesis.
These three dialectical laws therefore concern three different aspects of a being or concept—that is, three stages in its dialectical becoming.
But I repeat: all this is possible only because dialectical logic understands the law of “contradiction” positively rather than negatively, as traditional logic does.

Traditional logic treats non-A as a kind of “pure” negation with no positive content of its own. Such a negation is completely indefinite or, if you prefer, infinite. It has no particular connection with A. A “non-cat,” for example, could be absolutely anything: a dog, the sun, the square root of two, an ice cream, and so on.

If this is so, it is natural to assume that non-A cannot exist independently and cannot determine any particular aspect of being or any particular moment of becoming. An existing thing cannot exist as non-A. It must therefore exist only as A: it is equal to itself, that is, equal to A. A = A therefore cannot be B, much less C.
Hegel, however, noticed that things do not actually work this way—or at least not entirely this way.
For my part, I would say that they do not work this way always and everywhere. They work this way only in non-dialectical existence.
Purely at the formal level, we can expose the mistake in classical logic by pointing out that A itself enters into non-A and gives that negation its determinate character.
A “pure” negation—the isolated “not” by itself—is indeed indeterminate, infinite, and therefore incapable of being any particular entity. It is not something. It is nothing.

But non-A is not a “pure” negation or negation in general. It is, on the contrary, a completely determinate negation: specifically, the negation of A. It is therefore clearly distinct from the negation of M or N—that is, from non-M, non-N, and so on.

So all the determinations of A also relate in some way to non-A, which is itself determinate—that is, which is something determinate. And since non-A negates A, its determinations differ from those of A. It is therefore not A but B.
This B is itself bounded, delimited, determinate. In that sense it is something, just as A is. This is why it is also positive.
Yet B remains both the negation of A and the negation of A. It is therefore a particular result: the result of a particular process, namely the negation of A.
So even if we cannot say that A can be B, we can say that A can become B. B is a result. A becomes B when A negates itself.
But in B—that is, in non-A—A remains present in one way or another. It has been preserved.
We can therefore say that dialectical being can remain itself both when it affirms itself and when it negates itself: it can be, first, A and then B.

Yet insofar as it is both A and B, it is no longer simply non-A or simply non-B, since A and B negate and exclude one another. It is therefore a third thing, C, in which both A and B are preserved, though in a different form.
And since A and B are each fully determinate, C is determinate as well.

Once again, everything depends on non-A being equal to B—that is, to a particular determinate negation with a bounded and positive content of its own—and not to zero (0) or infinity (∞), as non-dialectical logic assumes.
So the whole question is this: is traditional logic right, or is Hegel?
A few simple examples will show that the issue is not nearly as easy to settle in favor of traditional logic as many aspiring philosophers imagine.

Suppose I say that the cover of a certain book “is not red.” Any “normal” person will assume that it is “blue,” “black,” or some other color. It would never occur to them, on the basis of what I said, that it might be a turtle, an integral, or a cloud.

In other words, if I negate a particular color, everyone understands that what I am determining through this negation is still a color and not something else. It is of course not this color, and not that color either, but neither is it a “non-color” in the sense of absolutely anything whatsoever.

Formal logic may quite reasonably object that this psychological observation proves nothing logically. A strictly logical mind should, in principle, understand “non-color” to include everything that is not color. Even so, this example makes the undeniable artificiality of the traditional understanding of negation perfectly clear.
There is another obvious weakness in it.

If I say of something that it “is not a dog,” I have obviously said very little about it. But I have still “determined” it in some way, and in a sense I have determined it “positively.” We now know positively that it “is not a dog.”
Very often, knowing that something is not a dog can be just as important as knowing what it actually is—especially if we are talking about food.
Now suppose I say that something “is not a cat.” Of course, this “non-dog” and this “non-cat” might turn out to be the same thing. The sun, for example, is neither a cat nor a dog.
Even so, “non-cat” is not exactly the same as “non-dog.” The former may perfectly well be a dog; the latter cannot possibly be one.
If this is so, then a determinate negation is itself a certain positive determination of whatever it applies to.

And if the number of possible determinations were finite, it would make no fundamental difference whether we defined things positively or negatively. If, for example, a book cover could only be red, blue, or black, it would make no difference whether we said that it was blue or that it was neither red nor black.
Traditional logic replies that the number of possible determinations is in fact infinite. Non-A therefore cannot have any determinate, or positive, content.
But even if the claim that there are infinitely many possibilities were justified, the conclusion still would not follow, as the next example shows.
Atheism is undeniably the negation of theism. The word itself says as much: a-theism means non-theism.
And the entire content of atheism seems to be concentrated in a single claim: God does not exist. In other words, anything whatsoever may exist except God; everything is “non-God.”
It might seem that such a thin negation could never produce a determinate, positive theory.
Experience shows otherwise. Atheism is just as determinate and positive a doctrine as theism—and it has the additional advantage of being true.
And insofar as the word “God” has any meaning at all, “a-theism” is just as meaningful and coherent as “theism.” Even the theist cannot deny this, since the theist argues with the atheist.
Later we will see that atheism itself fully determines a particular—and, moreover, true—doctrine of humanity.

Nothing essential about human beings follows from the fact that there are, for example, no centaurs. But a great deal follows from the non-existence of the Christian “God,” or indeed of any “gods” at all.
If one wished, one could derive the whole Hegelian-Marxist dialectical anthropology from the non-existence of “God,” just as one can derive the non-existence of God from that anthropology.

The mistake of traditional formal logic is precisely that it is formal—that is, abstract. Because it does not deal with actual reality, it cannot distinguish between what is merely possible—what exists “in potential”—and what is actual, what exists “in act.”
“In potential,” negation may indeed be “anything whatsoever.” It cannot therefore be determinate and so, strictly speaking, cannot be at all. In short, it is nothing.
But negation in act is always the negation of something determinate. The bare “not” becomes actual only in the form “not-A.”
And this determinate negation always appears as something both positive and determinate.

We can say of non-A that it cannot be A. So it is already no longer “anything whatsoever.” This means that we can say something about it. It is therefore not nothing but something. In some sense it exists and thus appears as something determinate.
All these abstract arguments will become fully convincing only once we establish the genuinely concrete meaning of the concepts we are using.
But since we already know that real “negativity” is realized, above all, through struggle—that is, through active or revolutionary negation—we can already see what is at stake.
There can be no doubt that the revolutionary negation of an existing reality opens up, through the revolutionaries who negate it, unlimited possibilities.

In actual reality, revolutionaries are constrained by the positive character of the regime they are overthrowing. The attempt to realize all the possibilities contained in revolutionary negation leads to disaster—“Trotskyism.”
Their indeterminacy and infinity conflict with the laws of finite existence. Such an “utopian” attempt therefore leads to “non-being.”
In this sense, formal logic is right: a “pure” negation cannot exist.
But insofar as the revolutionary is not a utopian—that is, insofar as he takes existing circumstances into account, as Lenin and Stalin did against Trotsky—he realizes the negation.
Those very circumstances limit what is possible and, by doing so, determine the outcome of the negation.
The result of the Revolution is therefore not the disappearance of the state, or “anarchy,” but a new and fully determinate form of state existence.
Non-A turns out to be B—and ultimately C.
In any case, once we accept the basic dialectical law of “positive” negation—the “positive law of contradiction”—we must also accept the “law of the included third.”
In other words, we must accept the dialectical triad: thesis, antithesis, synthesis.
We can therefore say that a dialectical concept, being, or entity always appears as precisely the “third” term excluded by formal, non-dialectical logic.
It is always a “synthesis”: not merely self-affirmation and not merely self-negation, but their union or mutual penetration.
Yet a synthesis is a synthesis only insofar as it includes the “antithesis.”
There is no necessary passage from the “thesis” as a law—that is, from the “law of identity”—to a “positive law of contradiction.”
If we examine or analyze the “law of identity” alone, we can derive from it only what non-dialectical logic derives: the negative law of non-contradiction and the law of the excluded third.

To transform the non-dialectical law of identity into the first and fundamental dialectical law—to turn A = A into a thesis—we must add the equally independent and equally “underivable” positive law of contradiction.
Once we have those two laws, we can derive a third and final basic dialectical law: the law of the included third.
So if every dialectical concept, being, and entity is always an “included third,” that is, a synthesis, this is only because it is also a “positive negation,” that is, an antithesis.
Once again, we see that the nerve of dialectic is “negativity.”
The meaning of the dialectical triad—or, if you prefer, the three-in-one structure of dialectical being—is easiest to see in the example of human speech.

It is therefore no accident that dialectic was first discovered by Plato in its discursive form, where it appears as “discussion,” and that until Hegel it was wrongly confined to discourse alone, as though it did not exist outside it at all.
Suppose someone makes a meaningful assertion, A.
It is always possible, though not necessary, to negate it—that is, to make an opposing assertion, non-A.
